answer.label: No documented source — unverified attribution to Zora Neale Hurston
answer.authorDates: 1891–1960 · American author, anthropologist & folklorist of the Harlem Renaissance
answer.sourceLine: This line is credited to Hurston almost everywhere online, but it appears in none of her documented novels, essays, folklore, letters, or interviews. No book, page, speech, or date has ever been produced — Goodreads carries its “not verified” disclaimer, WIST files it as merely “(Attributed),” and Wikiquote does not list it at all. Treat the attribution as unsourced.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: If you are silent about your pain, they’ll kill you and say you enjoyed it.
trail: Quote databases attach no citation: Goodreads shows the line under Hurston’s name but appends its standard notice that “Quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified,” and names no book — see the Goodreads entry.
The careful curators refuse to source it: WIST lists it only as “(Attributed)” with no work cited, and the sourced Wikiquote page for Hurston does not include it at all.
Where a book is named, it is wrong: the sentence does not appear in Their Eyes Were Watching God, the novel most often cited as its origin.
source.excerptNote: Circulated with no surrounding context — no chapter, page, essay, letter, or interview is ever attached to it.
source.rightsNote: Because no source work or date can be tied to this exact wording, its copyright status cannot be determined. This is not a claim of public domain: an unsourced line of unknown origin has no established first publication, so no rights status is asserted.

author.name: Zora Neale Hurston
author.heading: About Zora Neale Hurston
author.metaLine: 1891–1960 · American author, anthropologist & folklorist of the Harlem Renaissance
author.bio: Zora Neale Hurston (1891–1960) was a novelist, anthropologist, and folklorist whose fieldwork and fiction made her a central figure of the Harlem Renaissance; her best-known work is the 1937 novel Their Eyes Were Watching God. She died in obscurity in 1960 and was rediscovered in the 1970s largely through Alice Walker’s advocacy. Her fame — and the fact that so few readers have combed her full body of work — makes her a frequent magnet for punchy, uplifting lines she never actually wrote.

misattribution.heading: An attribution with no source
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared “Hurston” quotes on the internet, yet it rests on nothing. The credit is repeated confidently across quote sites, mugs, and social posts, but no one has ever produced the passage it supposedly comes from.

items.why: Near-universally credited to Hurston, but the line appears in none of her documented books, essays, folklore collections, letters, or interviews. WIST records it only as “(Attributed),” and Wikiquote omits it entirely.
When a source is named at all, it is usually this novel — but the sentence does not appear in its text. The claim adds false specificity to an attribution that has none.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: there is no documented source. Until a passage in Hurston’s own writing or a recorded remark surfaces, this should be treated as an unsourced attribution — a line the internet gave Hurston, not one she is shown to have written. See Wikiquote’s sourced list, which does not include it.

context.heading: Why it sticks to her name
lead: The line is vivid, defiant, and reads like hard-won wisdom about silence and survival — exactly the register readers associate with Hurston’s voice. That fit is why the attribution spreads so easily: it feels right, so few people stop to ask which book it came from.

But feeling right is not evidence. Hurston is a classic “quote magnet”: widely revered, endlessly excerpted, and read in full by relatively few, so aphorisms of uncertain origin drift toward her name and calcify there. The responsible position is to enjoy the sentiment while being clear that the attribution is unverified.
context.pull: It reads like Hurston — which is exactly why no one checks.
